Gothic Arc

GeometryCirclesTriangles
What it shows: Circles sit in a row between two curved arcs and a straight base.
How to play: Drag the two end dots to change the arcs, tick "names" to label the points, and choose Gothic arc or arbelos. Press Reset to start again.
Look for the math

The little circles look as if they were chosen one at a time by eye. In fact their sizes follow one simple rule, and the rule makes several right triangles with whole-number sides appear for free.

The curve and the chain

The Gothic arc OBC is made from two arcs of the same radius, one centred at O and one at B. Each circle in the picture touches the semicircle on OB, the Gothic arc, and the circle before it. The first two are called K and P; the applet builds seven circles in all. Its Apollonius calculation picks the tangent circle that stays inside the gap, and the test checks those tangencies for every drawn circle.

The arbelos in disguise

The same chain sits inside an arbelos, the shape bounded by three touching semicircles. Write R for the radius of the large semicircle and take the small radius as r = 1. The radius of the n-th circle is

Rn = Rr / (r2 + r + n2) = R / (2 + n2)

So R1 = R/3 and R2 = R/6, and their sum is R/2 = OD. That is why KP is parallel to the base and P lies directly above D, the midpoint of the right semicircle. Dividing by OD gives Rn/OD = 2/(2+n2): a rational number for every n. The logic test checks this exactly for n up to 60.

Right triangles for free

Let Pn be the point directly below the n-th centre. Pappus' chain gives OnPn = 2nRn, while the page's other two lengths are

DPn = (n2 − 4)R / [2(2 + n2)]
DOn = (n2 + 4)R / [2(2 + n2)]

Multiply the three sides by 2(2+n2)/R and they become n2−4, 4n, n2+4. Since (n2−4)2 + (4n)2 = (n2+4)2, every DPnOn is a Pythagorean triple. The test verifies that integer identity for n up to 200. The page's three named cases all check out: ODP is 3-4-5, n = 6 gives 24, 32, 40 over 76, and OP3O3 is 6, 8, 10.

The one-pixel quirk

The original applet puts the point O two pixels off centre and inflates each neighbour circle by one pixel before solving for the next one. Its drawn radii therefore drift slightly below the ideal fractions: in the default 500 by 400 picture they are 73.27 and 36.14, while R/3 = 73.33 and R/6 = 36.67. The formulas above are exactly true of the ideal chain the page describes, not of those buffered pixels. This page keeps the applet's construction in its drawing and tests both pictures separately.

Try dragging B towards A: the whole chain shrinks, but each radius stays the same fraction of OD. Then switch to the arbelos view and look for the 3-4-5 triangles without the Gothic arcs.
